evidence: Plaut. Men. 1157: Auctiō fīet Menaechmī māne sānē septimī
terms.comment: A sale to the highest bidder: a spear (hasta) was set up, a crier (praecō) called the bids and a banker took the money (Lewis & Short). To hold one, auctiōnem facere.

evidence: Liv. 23.38.7: comitibusque eōrum sub hastā vēnditīs, and their companions sold at auction
Caes. BG 1.18.3: illō licente contrā licērī audeat nēmō, no one dares bid against him
Cic. Verr. 2.3.27: quī digitō sit licitus, who bid with a raised finger
terms.comment: The goods themselves licent, fetch a price: vēnībunt quīquī licēbunt (Plaut. Men. 1159).

terms.gloss: the crier who calls an auction; an auctioneer
evidence: Hor. AP 419: ut praecō, ad mercēs turbam quī cōgit emendās, like a crier who gathers a crowd to buy the goods

phrases.latin: Auctiō fīet Menaechmī māne sānē septimī. vēnībunt servī, supellex, fundī, aedēs, omnia. vēnībunt quīquī licēbunt, praesentī pecūniā.
phrases.english: Menaechmus’s auction will be held bright and early on the seventh day. For sale: slaves, furniture, farms, house, everything. Sold at whatever they fetch, cash down.

sources: Lewis & Short: auctio · Lewis & Short: hasta · Lewis & Short: liceor · Lewis & Short: praeco
Plautus, Livy, Caesar, Cicero and Horace checked against the Latin Library texts (CLTK mirror) (9 November 2026).
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
